<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-articulated cases with genuine engagement, but B's case proved more resilient under pressure. B's "you can't buy a bus route that doesn't exist" turn on A's own heterogeneity argument exposed a real weakness in the cash model for thin markets that A's "demand creates supply" answer never fully repaired (A's own admission that "planners abandon thin markets too" muddied rather than resolved the point). B's "degraded service vs. zero service" asymmetry, introduced in Rebuttal 2, gave the debate a clean decision rule that A's closing reasserted prior points against but did not squarely dismantle. B also skillfully redirected A's "welfare states layer cash on top" concession into "nobody layers services on top of cash," a rhetorically effective reversal that landed in B's favor at the close. A had strong moments — sharp distinctions between network goods and individualized services, pointed pressure questions on accountability, and a clean tie-back to the proposition's exact wording in the final speech — but B's answers to those pressure questions, while imperfect (the "fixable by a budget vote" response to chronic decades-long deficits was somewhat hand-waved), were not exploited further by A in the closing. Both openings/rebuttals suffered one clipped turn each, roughly offsetting as execution costs. Overall B ends the exchange with the more durable framing and fewer unanswered structural weaknesses.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 turn ("the night-shift worker and rural parent don't get served better by cash either — you can't buy a bus route that doesn't exist") flipped A's central heterogeneity argument against cash, and A's subsequent "demand creates supply" response never fully closed that gap, especially once pressed by B's rural hospital/broadband question.</best_rebuttal>
